title: BDD, ADR, PRD, WTF: Capturing Decisions for Humans and AI Alike — Michal Cichra, Safe Intelligence

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk presents a framework for keeping AI coding agents on track through ADRs, PRDs, BDD/Cucumber, and infrastructure enforcement via git hooks and CI rather than prompt context.

summary: Michal Cichra opens with the monkey-banana experiment to illustrate that both humans and LLMs suffer from limited context: people forget, leave, and LLMs context compact with no persistent memory. This makes capturing decisions essential. He presents three complementary documents. ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) record why architectural decisions are made and how they are enforced—e.g., splitting code layers to prevent N+1 queries, enforcing that database reads return plain shapes instead of ORM objects, and linting module imports. ADRs are text documents that reference affected files and enforcement mechanisms; when agents are rejected at commit time, they are linked back to the ADR, read it, and iterate. PRDs (Product Requirements Documents) are lighter, capturing why a feature exists, what problem it solves, and the user journey through the application—useful for agents and for humans weeks later. BDD (Behavior-Driven Development) via Cucumber addresses the gap in spec-driven development: markdown specs describe behavior but do not verify it. Cucumber provides executable, human-readable scenarios that connect to PRDs and critical user journeys, parseable by step definitions into code. For UI consistency, he advocates design systems with documented language, rules such as only one primary button per page, and components with previews and snippets visible to agents. Enforcement uses a loop: git hooks run predefined tasks (linting, formatting, type checking, architecture checks, document linting) replicated in CI so agents cannot skip them. Different skills (ADR, PRD, UI, test) focus the loop while keeping its structure constant. The approach is context-heavy—half the context can vanish during research—but 20-50 context compacts per session work fine because important decisions survive in the codebase and agents look them up again.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & The Context Problem
sections.summary: Michal introduces himself and Safe Intelligence's newly released Spec 27. He uses the monkey-banana cage experiment to illustrate that both humans and LLMs suffer from limited context—people forget and leave, LLMs context compact and have no memory—causing teams to lose sight of why features and code exist.

sections.title: ADR — Architecture Decision Records
sections.summary: ADRs record why architectural decisions are made and how they are enforced. Examples include splitting code in layers to prevent N+1 queries, enforcing plain shapes from database reads instead of ORM objects, and linting module imports. ADRs are text documents referencing affected files and enforcement tools; when agents are rejected at commit time they get linked back to the ADR, read the rationale, and iterate.

sections.title: PRD — Product Requirements Documents
sections.summary: PRDs are lighter documents capturing why a feature exists, what problem it solves, and the user journey through the application. They need not be exhaustive—just the why, the problem, the goal, and the journey connecting them. They serve agents and humans alike, including the author six weeks later.

sections.title: BDD & Cucumber — Executable Specifications
sections.summary: Spec-driven development leaves a loop open: markdown specs describe behavior but do not verify it. BDD via Cucumber provides executable, human-readable scenarios that connect directly to PRDs and critical user journeys. Scenarios are parsed by step definitions and executed as code, but remain reviewable and understandable by humans, closing the spec verification gap.

sections.title: Design Systems for Consistent UI
sections.summary: Building consistent UIs with agents is another level of hard. Design systems and pattern libraries remain the solution. Document the language (e.g., primary button is blue, specific shape and size), define rules (only one primary button per page), create components with previews and snippets visible to agents, then compose and reuse them from small pieces to larger ones.

sections.title: Enforcement Loop — Git Hooks, CI, Linters & Skills
sections.summary: Enforcement uses a loop of git hooks, skills, CI, and linters. Git hooks run predefined tasks also executed in CI, so agents cannot skip them. Checks include linting, formatting, type checking, code duplication, architecture checks, and document linting. Architecture is enforced via module import separation—E2E tests cannot import database-accessing modules, templates cannot touch the database—making N+1 queries structurally impossible. Different skills (ADR, PRD, UI, test) focus the loop while keeping its structure constant.

sections.title: Drawbacks & Conclusion
sections.summary: The approach is context-heavy—half the context can vanish during research—but 20-50 context compacts per session are fine because important decisions survive in the codebase and agents look them up again. The goal is multi-hour autonomous sessions with clear goals and rules defined in infrastructure. Michal concludes by summarizing the toolkit: ADRs, PRDs, BDD/Cucumber, design systems, and the enforcement harness.
